finding.claim: Time-based claim validators are skipped when the claim is absent. With `maxAge` configured, a token with no `iat` claim is never checked against maxAge, so it stays valid indefinitely (fail-open). The same skip applies to `exp`: a token with no `exp` never expires.
finding.source: Attacker holds a validly signed token that lacks `iat` (issued by a signer with `noTimestamp: true`, or by any issuer that omits iat). The verifier is configured with `maxAge`.
finding.sink: verifyToken validator loop (verifier.js:312-331) returns success without applying the iat/maxAge check (verifier.js:648-650).

trace.note: createVerifier pushes the maxAge validator as {type:'date', claim:'iat', modifier: maxAge}
`if (!(claim in payload)) continue` skips the iat validator when the claim is missing
Cache hit path returns the cached result; cacheSet (verifier.js:137-140) also only bounds by iat when iat is a number, so the lifetime bound is never applied
cacheSet's maxAge bound is also gated on typeof payload.iat === 'number'

finding.guards_checked: Signature verification runs first (verifier.js:282-288), so the token must be genuinely signed by the key. requiredClaims (verifier.js:301-307) would reject the missing claim, but it is opt-in and not set by default. The maxAge validator is only added when maxAge is a number (verifier.js:648). No other path enforces the lifetime. Signature, alg, crit, and typ checks are not relevant to this issue.
finding.repro: Create a signer with noTimestamp: true and no expiresIn. Sign {sub:'u1'}. Create a verifier with key and maxAge: 60. Wait more than 60s and call verify(token). It returns the payload, even though maxAge should reject it. Setting requiredClaims: ['iat'] causes it to be rejected. Not executed: this environment has no shell, so the result is from reading the code only.

finding.claim: The library claims to reject non-canonical base64url, but the signature segment is decoded with Buffer.from(...,'base64'), which silently ignores the unused trailing bits. Each signature therefore has several distinct valid token strings, so token identity is malleable.
finding.source: Attacker holds one valid token (for example an HS256 token with a 43-char signature, where the last char has 2 unused bits, or an RS256 token with 4 unused bits in the last char).
finding.sink: Signature verification at verifier.js:177 -> verifySignature in crypto.js:394 (`Buffer.from(signature,'base64')`) and crypto.js:398 (timingSafeEqual). The malleable token string is accepted as a fresh, valid token.

trace.note: BASE64URL_RE is only an alphabet check; it does not check canonical padding bits
signature segment passes the alphabet check, so a last char that differs only in unused bits is accepted
validateAlgorithmAndSignature calls verifySignature with the raw signature string
Buffer.from(signature,'base64') decodes both canonical and non-canonical forms to the same bytes
HMAC timingSafeEqual succeeds for the same bytes; RSA/EC/Ed verification also succeeds for the same bytes
Comment asserts the signature is 'canonical' by this point. That is false for trailing bits.

finding.guards_checked: Decoder checks the alphabet and rejects padding and whitespace (decoder.js:10,35-43). The payload and header are malleable only in ways that change the signed input string, so they fail signature verification. Only the signature has the malleability. The cache is keyed by the raw token string, so it does not block variants. Impact requires an application that keys revocation, replay, or one-time-use state on the raw token string or its hash rather than on jti or the decoded signature bytes.
finding.repro: Take a valid HS256 token with a 43-char signature. Replace the last signature char with another char whose index differs only in the low 2 bits (for example 'B'->'C' in base64url, same decoded bytes). verify() still accepts it, and the string differs from the original. Not executed: this environment has no shell, so the result is from reading the code only.
